# Reproducing the SDPR V2 OCR Performance Report as a real workflow

**Status:** implementation brief / handoff
**Date:** 2026-07-29
**Base branch:** `develop`
**Ticket summary:** *"The report was generated by postprocessing the OCR data with local scripts. Construct a workflow that reproduces benchmark results and that can run in the operational setting. Include HITL criteria (currently there's no way to configure the rules for which fields get shown). To validate, compare the results from the workflow (ran via benchmark) to the report values, should align."*

---

## 0. The one-paragraph version

The SDPR V2 performance report's headline numbers (96.4% field accuracy, 267 errors, the HITL staffing tables) were **not** produced by this product. The product produced a weaker, "strict" set of numbers; a stack of local Python scripts then post-processed that export — relaxing format-only mismatches, recovering income zeros that Azure misread as checkboxes, and sizing the human-review workload. Your job is to move that post-processing **inside the application**: the parts that change data belong in the workflow (so production documents actually carry the corrected values), the parts that are purely about how we *score* belong in the benchmark's evaluator config, and the human-review policy becomes a new, configurable workflow node. When you're done, running the benchmark on the same 99 documents should produce the report's numbers **directly from the export**, with no Python normalisation step in between. That match is the proof the workflow is correct.

---

## 1. Background — what the report is and why this ticket exists

### 1.1 The document under study

SDPR (Ministry of Social Development and Poverty Reduction) processes a paper form: the **HR0081 Monthly Report**. Clients fill it in by hand. It carries 75 extractable fields per form:

| Category | Fields | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| `income_amounts` | 35 | 18 applicant lines + 17 spouse lines. **Most cells are a hand-written `0`** meaning "no income from this category". |
| `checkboxes` | 28 | yes/no pairs |
| `name`, `sin`, `phone`, `date`, `signature` | 2 each | applicant + spouse |
| `case_id` | 1 | |
| `freeform_text` (`explain_changes`) | 1 | free-form paragraph |

Today SDPR staff key every field of every form by hand, roughly 35,000 reports/month. The product being built OCRs the form and routes only *some* fields to a human. The report exists to answer: *is that accurate enough to be worth doing, and how much human review does it actually cost?*

### 1.2 What was benchmarked

99 production documents, each with hand-labelled ground truth (GT). Two engines:

- **V1 — Azure DI custom *template* model.** Finds fields by fixed position. Trained on 9 real + 6 synthetic docs. Fragile against rotation, cropping, stamps. 88.8% accuracy.
- **V2 — Azure DI custom *neural* model.** Learns visual features instead of positions. Trained on 60 production documents. This is the current engine.

The report shows V2 in **two scoring views**, and understanding this split is the whole ticket:

| Column | What it is | Accuracy | Where it came from |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Template (V1) | baseline | 88.8% | in-app benchmark export |
| **Neural V2 strict** | V2's raw output, scored with strict string equality | 91.6% | **in-app benchmark export** |
| **Neural V2 current** | *the same predictions*, after offline normalisation + zero recovery | **96.4%** | **local Python scripts** |

The 4.8-point gap between "strict" and "current" is entirely post-processing that lives outside the product. That gap is what this ticket closes.

### 1.3 What the local scripts actually do

They live in [`scripts/benchmark analysis/`](../../scripts/benchmark%20analysis/) (already on `develop`). Read [`SDPR_V2_REPORT_PIPELINE.md`](../../scripts/benchmark%20analysis/SDPR_V2_REPORT_PIPELINE.md) — it is the authoritative description. In short:

1. **`normalize-benchmark.py`** — walks the benchmark export and flips errors to "matched" when the mismatch is format-only. E.g. predicted `$2,711.64` vs GT `2711.64`; predicted `2026-Mar-16` vs GT `2026-03-16`; predicted `999888777` vs GT `999-888-777`. Writes an audit CSV naming the rule behind every flip.
2. **`recover-numeric-zeros.py`** — the biggest single lever (~+4 of the +4.8 points). Azure's layout pass often reads a hand-written `0` as a *selection mark* (a checkbox), so the income field arrives **blank**. This script finds the income table in the OCR layout, maps cells to field keys, and where a cell is empty *and* a selection-mark polygon overlaps it, sets the value to `0`.
3. **`hitl-planner.py`** — sizes the human review workload. For each of six target recall levels it picks the confidence threshold that catches that fraction of errors and reports reviews-per-100-documents. This produces the §10.5 staffing tables.
4. **`compare-engines.py` / `analyze.js` / `report-errors.py`** — the tables, plots and per-error audit CSVs in the report.

### 1.4 Why "in the app" matters, not just "reproducible"

The scripts are reproducible today. The problem is that **only two of the three things they do are legitimate as post-processing:**

- Deciding `$2,711.64` and `2711.64` are the same number is a *scoring* judgement — fine to make at evaluation time.
- Deciding a blank income cell is really a `0` **changes the data**. In production, the `0` has to be in the record that reaches the caseworker's review screen and the downstream system. A scorer that quietly forgives the blank produces a good-looking benchmark and a broken product.
- Deciding which fields a human reviews is *operational policy*. It currently exists only inside a Python script's CLI flags. Production has no equivalent — see §1.5.

So: **the offline normaliser flips scores; the workflow has to flip values.** Sorting each rule into "workflow" or "evaluator" is the central design act of this ticket, and §5 does it rule by rule.

### 1.5 The HITL half of the ticket

The ticket's second sentence — *"currently there's no way to configure the rules for which fields get shown"* — is literally true:

- Whether a document needs review is decided by [`ocr.checkConfidence`](../../apps/temporal/src/activities/check-ocr-confidence.ts), which averages **every word confidence on the page** and compares it to one number (default 0.95). It is document-level and field-blind.
- The review screen then shows **every** field in the document's OCR result, sorted by confidence (`HitlService.getSession` returns `ocr_result.keyValuePairs` wholesale).

The report models something completely different: review is **scoped to `income_amounts` and `sin`**, with an **independent confidence threshold per category**, and two prediction shapes filtered out before they ever reach a reviewer. None of that is expressible in the product. You are building the mechanism that makes it expressible — generically, not hard-coded to SDPR.

## 2. Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Ground truth (GT)** | The hand-labelled correct values for a document, stored as JSON per sample. |
| **Prediction** | What the engine returned for a field. |
| **Cell** | One `(document, field)` pair. 99 docs × 75 fields ≈ 7,425 cells. |
| **missing** | GT has a value, prediction is blank. Also called a deletion. |
| **extra** | GT is blank, prediction has a value. A hallucination / phantom extraction. |
| **wrong** | Both have values and they differ. A substitution. Counts as *both* a false positive and a false negative. |
| **Accuracy** | matched cells ÷ all evaluated cells. The headline number. |
| **Recall (HITL sense)** | Of all errors present, what fraction did the review gate flag? Distinct from the metric of the same name in §10.2. |
| **Reviews per 100 docs** | The workload metric: how many predictions a human must look at, per 100 documents. |
| **Normalisation** | Treating two different-looking values as equivalent. |
| **Recovery** | Reconstructing a value the engine failed to emit at all. |
| **Selection mark** | Azure's term for a checkbox glyph. Central to the zero-recovery problem. |
| **Benchmark definition** | A saved combination of {dataset version, pinned workflow version, evaluator type, evaluator config}. Running one produces a **benchmark run**. |
| **`cleanedResultRef`** | The workflow context key holding the post-correction OCR result. **The benchmark scores this in preference to the raw result** — which is precisely the hook that makes in-workflow correction show up in the numbers. |

## 3. The target — numbers you must land on

These come from report §10.2, §10.3, §10.4 and §10.5.1. Treat them as the acceptance criteria.

### 3.1 Aggregates (99 docs, 7,425 predictions)

| Metric | Target (V2 current) |
|---|---:|
| Accuracy | **96.4%** |
| Precision | **97.8%** |
| Recall | **97.0%** |
| F1 | **0.974** |
| Avg false-positives per document | **1.66** |

### 3.2 Error classes

| Class | Target |
|---|---:|
| missing | **103** |
| extra | **46** |
| wrong | **118** |
| **Total** | **267** |

### 3.3 Per-category accuracy

| Category | n fields | Target |
|---|---:|---:|
| `name` | 2 | 0.96 |
| `freeform_text` | 1 | 0.99 |
| `signature` | 2 | 0.91 |
| `date` | 2 | 0.93 |
| `case_id` | 1 | 0.91 |
| `sin` | 2 | 0.89 |
| `phone` | 2 | 0.90 |
| `income_amounts` | 35 | 0.957 |
| `checkboxes` | 28 | 0.991 |

### 3.4 HITL ladder (report §10.5.1)

Scope: `income_amounts` + `sin` only. Per-category thresholds chosen independently.

| Target recall | T (sin) | sin reviews/100 | T (income) | income reviews/100 | **Combined reviews/100** | **Residual errors/100** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 50% | 0.61 | 13 | 0.61 | 28 | **41** | **45.5** |
| 70% | 0.70 | 21 | 0.75 | 50 | **71** | **26.3** |
| 80% | 0.72 | 25 | 0.89 | 70 | **95** | **15.2** |
| 90% | 0.90 | 50 | 0.96 | 99 | **149** | **8.1** |
| 95% | 0.97 | 96 | 0.97 | 109 | **205** | **3.0** |
| 99% | 0.99 | 98 | 0.98 | 140 | **238** | **0.0** |

§10 legitimately excludes two populations from this math, and you must preserve both exclusions or the numbers won't reconcile:

- **82 confidently-blank income cells.** The model returns blank *with high confidence* on 82 cells where the form has a value. No confidence threshold can reach them; they are the residual the zero-recovery layer doesn't catch. Excluded from HITL scope entirely.
- **Blank and single-character income predictions** are filtered out before the workload count (see §5.4 and §8.6).

After both exclusions the in-scope error pool is **22 sin errors + 68 income errors = 90**.

## 4. Where the work lands, and what already exists

### 4.1 Branch reality

You are building on **`develop`**. Be aware of what `develop` does and does not have, because a lot of workflow tooling exists on an unmerged branch:

| Capability | On `develop`? |
|---|---|
| Graph workflow engine (activity / switch / map / join / **humanGate** / pollUntil / childWorkflow nodes) | ✅ |
| Backend workflow module, versioning, config-hash pinning | ✅ |
| Benchmark: definitions pin a **workflow version**, runs execute that workflow per sample | ✅ |
| `evaluatorConfig` with per-field matching rules | ✅ |
| Reference data tables + `tables.lookup` activity | ✅ |
| Local-folder dataset seeding (`data/datasets/…`) | ✅ |
| The analysis scripts in `scripts/benchmark analysis/` | ✅ (identical to the branch they were written on) |
| **Visual workflow builder (canvas UI)** | ❌ — lives on `feature/visual-workflow-builder` (PR #230), ~541 commits ahead |
| **Dynamic / custom code nodes + `deno-runner`** | ❌ — same branch |

**Practical consequence:** you author workflows as **JSON configs** (the `docs-md/workflows/templates/*.json` pattern, seeded via `apps/shared/prisma/seed.ts`) and push them through the workflow API. There is no canvas, and no code-node escape hatch. See §6 for why that's fine — and actually the outcome we want.

### 4.2 PR #169 already builds the hardest piece

**[PR #169 — `feat(ocr): recover numeric zeros misread as checkboxes`](https://github.com/bcgov/ai-adoption-document-intelligence/pull/169)** (draft, branch `fix/temporal-pg-storage-quota`, targets `develop`) implements the zero-recovery step as a **first-class activity and node**, not a script. It contains:

- `apps/temporal/src/activities/ocr-recover-numeric-zeros.ts` + tests — activity `ocr.recoverNumericZerosFromCheckboxes`
- Registration in both activity registries and the graph schema validator
- `apps/temporal/src/types.ts` — adds `selectionMarks?: SelectionMark[]` to `Page` (the app previously **dropped** selection marks, which is why the Python had to read the raw Azure cache instead)
- `docs-md/extraction/OCR_RECOVER_NUMERIC_ZEROS.md` — full algorithm documentation
- `docs-md/workflows/templates/standard-ocr-workflow-sdpr.json` — a seeded SDPR variant workflow with the node wired in
- Seed wiring for the variant workflow

The node implements all three table-finder strategies the Python has (title anchor, row-label anchor, positional anchor), is blob-backed like the other correction activities (reads `ocrResultRef`, writes a new ref, never mutates its input), and is a **no-op when no table config is supplied** — so it is safe in generic workflows.

**Your first task is therefore not to build zero recovery. It is to rebase, review, verify and land PR #169.** Check in particular:

1. That the recovery numbers match the Python's. The Python's audit rows are tagged `recovered:checkbox-zero`, `recovered:checkbox-zero-label-anchor`, `recovered:checkbox-zero-positional` — count them in `benchmark-result-neural-normalized.changes.csv` and compare against the node's per-strategy counts on the same documents. The report expects **~120 recovered cells**.
2. That `azureOcr.extract` really passes `selectionMarks` through (it does `pages: analyzeResult.pages || []`, so it does once the type admits the field — but confirm with a real response).
3. That the SDPR table config in the node's `parameters.tables` matches `SDPR_TABLE_CONFIG` in `recover-numeric-zeros.py` row-for-row.

The workflow template in that PR is your starting skeleton:

```
prepareFileData → submitOcr → updateApimRequestId → pollOcrResults → extractResults
  → recoverNumericZeros → postOcrCleanup → checkConfidence → reviewSwitch
      ├─(needs review)→ humanReview ─┐
      └─(no review)─────────────────┴→ storeResults
```

| Need | Existing generic mechanism |
|---|---|
| Per-field value canonicalisation (digits-only SIN, currency stripping, date format) | `format_spec` on each field in the TemplateModel's field schema, applied by the **`ocr.normalizeFields`** node when given `documentType` = template model id. Engine: [`field-format-engine.ts`](../../apps/temporal/src/field-format-engine.ts), ops `digits`, `uppercase`, `lowercase`, `strip-spaces`, `text`, `number`, `date:FORMAT`, plus an optional `pattern` and `displayTemplate`. |
| Signature scored on presence, not characters | Evaluator rule `presence` — already config-driven |
| Date compared as a calendar date | Evaluator rule `date` (`parseToCalendarParts`) |
| Currency/number-tolerant comparison | Evaluator rule `numeric` (currency-aware parse) |
| GT cells that must not be scored | `:garbled:` wildcard sentinel, already honoured |
| Standard precision/F1 (substitution = FP **and** FN) | **Already fixed on `develop`** (commit `06dfdcbbb`). The report's §10.1.5 note claiming production still uses the old formula is **stale** — do not re-do this. |
| Where evaluator config lives for a form-specific workflow | The workflow template's `metadata.evaluatorConfig`; the seed lifts it into the benchmark definition. See `experiment-01-neural-doc-intelligence-workflow.json` for the shape. |
| Looking a record up in an external reference dataset at runtime | `tables.lookup` over a group-scoped reference table ([TABLES.md](../architecture/TABLES.md)) |
| Getting sample documents into a dev environment | Local-folder dataset seeding, `data/datasets/<name>/{public,private}/` ([local-datasets-seeding.md](../local-datasets-seeding.md)) |

## 5. The rule-by-rule split: workflow vs evaluator

This is the core design table. **Workflow** = the value is changed, and production sees the change. **Evaluator** = only the comparison is relaxed; the stored value is untouched.

| Offline rule | What it did | Lands in | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| `digits-only` (`sin`, `spouse_sin`, `phone`, `spouse_phone`) | ignore punctuation | **Workflow** | `format_spec: {"canonicalize":"digits","pattern":"^\\d{9}$"}` + `ocr.normalizeFields`. Plus evaluator canonicalisation — see §5.2. |
| `case-id-normalized` | ignore whitespace + case | **Workflow** | `format_spec: {"canonicalize":"strip-spaces\|uppercase"}` |
| `date-calendar` | same calendar date, any format | **Workflow + evaluator** | workflow: `{"canonicalize":"date:YYYY-MM-DD"}`; evaluator: `{"rule":"date"}` |
| `date-month-day-swap` | accept transposed month/day | **Neither — drop it.** | See §5.3 |
| `currency-chrome`, `numeric-equality` | `$2,711.64` ≡ `2711.64` | **Workflow + evaluator** | workflow: `{"canonicalize":"number"}`; evaluator: `{"rule":"numeric"}` |
| `income-single-char-zero`, `income-single-digit-to-zero` | a single character on an income cell means `0` | **Workflow** (decided — see §8.3) | new normalisation rule; business-approved |
| `recovered:checkbox-zero*` | blank + overlapping selection mark ⇒ `0` | **Workflow** | `ocr.recoverNumericZerosFromCheckboxes` (PR #169) |
| `signature-presence` | any non-empty pair matches | **Evaluator** | `{"rule":"presence"}` — already exists |
| `name-fuzzy`, `text-normalized` (names) | close-enough names match | **Evaluator** | `{"rule":"fuzzy"}` **+ a new `maxEdits` option** — see §8.4 |
| `freeform-fuzzy` | close-enough paragraphs match | **Evaluator** | same, `maxEdits: 4` |
| `checkbox-tag` (`:selected:` ≡ `selected`) | bridge two representations | **Neither — fix the representation.** | See §5.1 |

### 5.1 Checkbox tag equivalence — a benchmarking artifact, not an operational rule

**Your instinct is right: this should not exist.** Here is where it came from.

When a selection-mark field is exported for Azure DI *labelling*, the app writes the value in Azure's tag syntax — `template-model.service.ts` does exactly `text = label.value === "selected" ? ":selected:" : ":unselected:"`. Ground truth derived from that labelling therefore carries `:selected:`. But at *runtime*, `extractAzureFieldDisplayValue` renders the model's `valueSelectionMark` as the plain string `"selected"`. So GT says `:selected:` and the prediction says `selected`, and 2,772 checkbox cells all mismatch on punctuation.

That is purely a **representation inconsistency between the labelling export and the runtime output**. It has no operational meaning at all. Do **not** port a `checkbox-tag` scoring rule.

**How big is it?** Small — and the report's own numbers tell you so. The `checkboxes` category scores **0.989 under strict scoring** (i.e. with no `checkbox-tag` rule at all) and 0.991 with it. Across 28 fields × 99 documents = 2,772 cells, that is a difference of roughly **5–6 cells**. So the two representations already agree almost everywhere; the tag form leaks into only a handful of cells. That is consistent with it being an incidental artifact rather than a systemic mismatch — and it means the fix is cheap and low-risk. It is still worth doing at the source rather than carrying a scoring rule for it: five cells of scoring debt today is a whole category of confusion the first time someone changes the labelling export.

Fix it properly instead:

1. **Pick one canonical form** for selection-mark values — recommend the plain `selected` / `unselected` that the runtime already emits.
2. **Normalise ground truth once**, at the point GT is ingested or seeded, so stored GT uses the canonical form. (This is a data migration on the dataset, not a scoring hack. See §5.2 for the general shape of this decision.)
3. **Assert it**: add a test that the labelling-export tag form and the runtime form round-trip to the same canonical value, so the two representations can't silently diverge again.

Also worth confirming with the team, because it's cheap to check and would be a genuine bug if true: does the **labelling export** need `:selected:` (Azure's requirement), while everything else should use the plain form? If so the tag form is correct *only* at that one boundary and should be converted there and nowhere else.

Confirm the ~5-cell estimate against the audit CSV in P0 (`grep -c 'checkbox-tag'`) before you rely on it. If the real count is much larger than that, the strict-vs-current category gap doesn't explain it, and something else is going on — stop and work out what.

### 5.2 The canonicalisation-vs-ground-truth problem (expanded)

This deserves a careful explanation because it's the subtlest thing in the ticket.

**The situation.** Once the workflow canonicalises a value, the value in the pipeline is no longer the value the OCR emitted. Say the form has `999-888-777` written on it:

- Azure returns `"999 888 777"`.
- Your `ocr.normalizeFields` step, driven by `format_spec: {"canonicalize":"digits"}`, turns it into `"999888777"`.
- Ground truth, labelled by a human who typed what they saw, says `"999-888-777"`.
- The evaluator does a string comparison. **It fails.** You have made the pipeline better and the benchmark worse.

The offline normaliser dodged this by never touching values — it just declared the pair equivalent at scoring time. You can't dodge it, because production needs the canonical value.

**Three ways out.**

- **(a) Canonicalise both sides at scoring time.** Extend `FieldMatchingRule` with an optional `canonicalize` spec (a `FormatSpec`, the same shape `format_spec` already uses). The evaluator applies it to *both* prediction and GT before comparing. GT files are never touched.
  - *Pros:* generic and reusable for every future dataset; GT stays as labelled (auditable — you can always see what the human actually wrote); one implementation shared with the workflow, so the workflow and the scorer can never drift; works for datasets stored in the database or blob storage, where rewriting GT files isn't practical.
  - *Cons:* a small evaluator change; the config has to be kept in step with the workflow's `format_spec` values (mitigate by referencing the same spec strings).
- **(b) Rewrite / widen the ground truth.** There's precedent: `promote-gt-format-variants.ts` walks a benchmark run and promotes GT scalars to *one-of arrays* (`["999-888-777", "999888777"]`), which the evaluator already understands. So GT gains an alternate rather than losing the original.
  - *Pros:* no evaluator change; the evaluator's one-of support already exists.
  - *Cons:* it only writes local `data/datasets/**` GT files, so it does **not** help the production dataset this benchmark uses; it makes GT depend on which engine you happened to run; every new canonical form means another GT rewrite; and mutating GT while validating against a report whose numbers were computed from the *un*-mutated GT is exactly the mid-flight change §10.2 warns about.
- **(c) Make the workflow emit GT's format.** `format_spec` supports a `displayTemplate` (`###-###-###`), so the workflow could emit `999-888-777` and match GT verbatim.
  - *Pros:* zero evaluator change.
  - *Cons:* it makes the *production* data format a hostage to how labellers happened to type. GT is not consistent across the 99 samples — inconsistency is precisely why `digits-only` existed. And ICM wants digits, not punctuation.

**Recommendation: (a), with one exception.** Add `canonicalize?: FormatSpec` to `FieldMatchingRule` and apply it symmetrically. It is generic, it is small, it removes an entire class of format-only errors permanently for every dataset, and it keeps GT immutable during validation — which the alignment check depends on.

The exception is **checkboxes (§5.1)**, where the mismatch is not a formatting preference but two different serialisations of the same enum coming out of our own code. That one gets fixed at the source, once, not accommodated at scoring time.

### 5.3 `date-month-day-swap` (expanded)

**What the rule does.** If GT says `2026-07-03` and the engine says `2026-03-07` — same year, month and day transposed, both valid calendar dates — the offline normaliser scores it as a match.

**Why it existed.** Hand-written dates on the form appear in every format imaginable. Labellers normalised what they saw; the engine emitted its own reading. When both readings are structurally valid, there is genuinely no way from the data alone to tell whether the labeller read `3 July` and the engine read `7 March`, or the reverse. The rule was a pragmatic "don't punish the engine for an ambiguity we created".

**Why not to port it.** It accepts a *different calendar date* as correct. The app's existing `date` rule already handles the honest half of the problem — `2026-Mar-16` ≡ `2026-03-16`, `16/03/2026` ≡ `2026-03-16` — because `parseToCalendarParts` disambiguates by month validity wherever it can. The only cells `date-month-day-swap` adds are exactly the ones where **both** interpretations are valid, i.e. the ones where we have no evidence the engine was right. The report itself marks the entire `date` policy **provisional** and says it will likely be tightened once the field's downstream role is defined. Building a rule you already expect to delete is waste, and shipping "two different dates count as equal" into a benefits system is a bad default.

**Recommendation: drop the rule, and measure the cost.**

1. Count the flips: `grep -c 'date-month-day-swap' <changes.csv>` on the share.
2. `date` + `spouse_date` is 2 fields × 99 docs = 198 cells, so each flip is ≈0.5pp of the `date` category and ≈0.013pp of headline accuracy. Report the delta explicitly in your validation write-up rather than hiding it.
3. Fix the root cause instead: give `date` a `format_spec` of `{"canonicalize":"date:YYYY-MM-DD"}` so the pipeline emits one unambiguous format, and raise the affected GT cells with whoever owns labelling. They fall in the same bucket as the ~10 known-wrong GT cells (§10.3 below).

If the count turns out to be large enough to move the `date` category materially, don't silently absorb it — bring it back to Alex as a decision, with the number attached.

### 5.4 The two HITL prediction filters

The report's HITL model drops two prediction shapes before they reach a reviewer *or* the workload count:

- **Blank predictions.** If the model returned nothing, there's no value for the reviewer to verify against. In this dataset every wrong-blank income prediction corresponded to a cell whose true value was `0`, which the recovery layer targets instead.
- **Single-character income predictions.** These are auto-converted to `0` (§8.3) and never shown.

Both are **prediction-side only** — they require no knowledge of the correct answer — so they are implementable identically in production and in benchmark. That property is non-negotiable for anything you put in the criteria node: *if a rule needs the ground truth to make its decision, it cannot ship.* See §10.2 for the one place the report's own tooling breaks this rule and what it costs you.

## 6. Node strategy — build generic, avoid one-offs

Ordered preference, strictest first. This is policy, not a suggestion:

1. **Use an existing node.** If `ocr.normalizeFields`, `document.validateFields`, `tables.lookup`, `data.transform`, `ocr.enrich` or a switch can express it — use it, and put the specificity in *configuration* (field schema, `format_spec`, node parameters, reference table rows). Most of the normalisation ruleset lands here.
2. **Build a new generic node.** If the capability is genuinely missing but would serve other forms and other customers — build it properly: an activity, registry entry, parameter schema, tests, catalog docs. The HITL criteria node (§8.6) is exactly this. So was zero recovery: note that PR #169 built a *generic* table-mapped recovery node whose SDPR-ness lives entirely in `parameters.tables`, and deliberately kept the base workflow template free of it. Copy that pattern.
3. **A custom (dynamic) code node — last resort only.** Dynamic nodes let a user write code inline instead of adding an activity. **They are not on `develop`** — they arrive with the visual-workflow-builder branch. Reserve them for logic that is genuinely one-off and specific to a single customer's single form, where generalising would be invented complexity.

**If you hit case 3 before dynamic nodes ship:** implement it as a *temporary, clearly-marked* activity — named and documented as a placeholder, with a comment pointing at this brief — with the explicit intent that it is deleted and re-expressed as a dynamic node once that capability lands. Do not let a temporary one-off quietly become part of the permanent generic catalog. Every such node should be listed in your handoff notes so the swap is a tracked task, not an archaeology exercise.

For this ticket, my read is that **nothing needs case 3**. Everything below is either configuration of an existing node or a generic new node worth having.

Two standing repo rules that bind here (from `CLAUDE.md`):

- **No document-specific implementation.** The system must support arbitrary workloads. "SDPR" may appear in *configuration and seeded templates*; it must not appear in activity logic.
- **No placeholders or stubs for future use.** Build what the ticket asks for, completely. Where you find a gap, record it in your summary notes rather than half-building for it.

## 7. Phase plan

Each phase has an acceptance criterion you can actually check. Don't advance on faith.

### P0 — Access, inputs, and sizing (before writing code)

1. Get access to the network share folder and to the production instance (§9).
2. Copy down the input inventory in §9.1.
3. **Size every rule.** The audit CSV `benchmark-result-neural-normalized.changes.csv` has one row per flipped cell with a `rule` column. Produce a count per rule:

   ```bash
   # PII-safe: counts only, never print the value columns
   awk -F, 'NR>1 {print $3}' changes.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
   ```

   This tells you, before you build anything, exactly how many cells each rule is worth. It is also your per-rule regression target: when your workflow reproduces rule X, the number of cells it changes should match this count.

**Acceptance:** you have a table of `rule → cell count` totalling the gap between 623 strict errors and 267 current errors, and you can name which rules you are porting, which you are dropping (§5.1, §5.3), and what each dropped one costs.

### P1 — Land the zero-recovery node (PR #169)

Rebase onto current `develop`, review, verify against the Python (§4.2), fill any test gaps, merge.

**Acceptance:** a benchmark run of the seeded SDPR variant workflow, replaying the original OCR cache, drops the `missing` count from **225 → ~103** with no other change in place. That single number is the whole of the recovery layer's contribution.

### P2 — In-workflow field normalisation

Populate `format_spec` on the SDPR template model's field schema and wire `ocr.normalizeFields` into the workflow with `documentType` set to the template model id. Field-by-field specs in §8.2.

**Acceptance:** SIN/phone/case_id/date/income cells emerge in one canonical form; the corresponding `digits-only`, `case-id-normalized`, `currency-chrome`, `numeric-equality` and `date-calendar` rows in the audit CSV are all accounted for — either the workflow now produces a matching value, or the evaluator's symmetric canonicalisation (§5.2a) covers it.

### P3 — Income single-character → `0`

Approved as a workflow transformation (§8.3). Build it as a rule with an audit trail, not a silent coercion.

**Acceptance:** cell count matches the sum of `income-single-char-zero` + `income-single-digit-to-zero` from P0.

### P4 — Evaluator changes

`maxEdits` on the fuzzy rule; `canonicalize` on `FieldMatchingRule`; SDPR `evaluatorConfig` written into the workflow template's `metadata.evaluatorConfig`. Details in §8.4.

**Acceptance:** `name`, `spouse_name`, `explain_changes`, `signature`, `spouse_signature` categories hit their §3.3 targets.

### P5 — Checkbox representation fix

Per §5.1: canonical form, GT normalisation at ingest, round-trip test.

**Acceptance:** `checkboxes` category = 0.991 with **no** checkbox-specific scoring rule in `evaluatorConfig`. Without the representation fix you land on 0.989 (≈5 cells short) — small, but it is 5 of the 267 errors you're reconciling, so don't wave it through.

### P6 — HITL criteria node + review surface

The genuinely new feature. Full spec in §8.6 / §8.7.

**Acceptance:** running the workflow with the 90%-recall configuration flags the same field population the report's planner does — reconcile against `hitl/hitl-per-category.csv`, allowing for the documented sin-workload divergence in §10.2.

### P7 — Post-HITL simulated ICM handoff

Terminal step after the human gate (or after the gate is skipped). Spec in §8.8.

**Acceptance:** every document ends in a terminal state with a persisted handoff payload, whether or not it went through review.

### P8 — Validation and write-up

§10. Run the alignment benchmark, reconcile per-cell, document every delta.

## 8. Component specifications

### 8.1 The workflow

Start from `docs-md/workflows/templates/standard-ocr-workflow-sdpr.json` (PR #169) and extend to:

```
prepareFileData
  → submitOcr → updateApimRequestId → pollOcrResults → extractResults
  → recoverNumericZeros            (ocr.recoverNumericZerosFromCheckboxes)
  → normalizeFields                (ocr.normalizeFields, documentType = SDPR template model)
  → postOcrCleanup                 (ocr.cleanup)
  → reviewCriteria                 (NEW: hitl.applyReviewCriteria)
  → reviewSwitch                   (switch on requiresReview)
      ├─ true  → humanReview (humanGate) → icmHandoff
      └─ false →                            icmHandoff
  → storeResults / updateStatus
```

Ordering notes that matter:

- **Recovery before normalisation.** Recovery writes raw `0` values; normalisation then canonicalises them alongside everything else.
- **Criteria after all corrections.** The review policy must see final values and final confidences, otherwise you flag cells that a later step would have fixed.
- **Criteria before the switch.** The switch branches on the criteria node's output, replacing today's document-average confidence check as the routing signal.
- Keep `ocr.checkConfidence` only if something still needs a document-level average. The criteria node supersedes it for routing.

Keep the **base** `standard-ocr-workflow.json` untouched and generic. All SDPR specifics live in the variant template's node `parameters` and in the template model's field schema.

### 8.2 `format_spec` per field

`format_spec` is a JSON string on each `FieldDefinition` row. Grammar in [FIELD_FORMAT_ENGINE.md](./FIELD_FORMAT_ENGINE.md); ops are pipe-chained left to right.

| Field(s) | Proposed `format_spec` | Replaces offline rule |
|---|---|---|
| `sin`, `spouse_sin` | `{"canonicalize":"digits","pattern":"^\\d{9}$"}` | `digits-only` |
| `phone`, `spouse_phone` | `{"canonicalize":"digits","pattern":"^\\d{10}$"}` | `digits-only` |
| `case_id` | `{"canonicalize":"strip-spaces\|uppercase"}` | `case-id-normalized` |
| `date`, `spouse_date` | `{"canonicalize":"date:YYYY-MM-DD"}` | `date-calendar` |
| all 35 income fields | `{"canonicalize":"number"}` | `currency-chrome`, `numeric-equality` |
| `name`, `spouse_name`, `explain_changes` | `{"canonicalize":"text"}` | `text-normalized` |

Two things to verify while you do this:

- `pattern` is used for *validation*, and validation failure is a first-class HITL trigger (§8.6). A SIN that doesn't canonicalise to 9 digits is exactly the kind of cell a human should see. Wire that through rather than letting the pattern sit unused.
- `ocr.normalizeFields` also has per-rule toggles (whitespace, digit grouping, date separators, unicode, dehyphenation, comma-thousands, currency spacing) and a `fieldScope`. Prefer the field-schema `format_spec` route for anything field-specific; use the toggles only for document-wide hygiene.

### 8.3 Income single-character → `0`

**Decision: implemented in the workflow (option (a)).** This writes a real `0` into the data.

The report is explicit about the trade-off, and you should carry that wording into the code comment and the docs: *the vast majority of income cells on this form are `0`; cells where a single character was predicted overwhelmingly correspond to faint or off-centre `0` glyphs the OCR misread; the cost is that a legitimate single-digit income (e.g. `$9`) would be silently read as `0`.* SDPR has accepted this.

Requirements:

- **Scoped, not global.** It applies to numeric/income fields, selected by configuration (field type or explicit field list) — never to every field.
- **Configurable and off by default.** A generic `singleCharacterToZero`-style rule on the normalisation node, enabled by the SDPR variant's parameters.
- **Audited.** Every coercion emits a change record (field, before, after, rule name) the same way the other correction activities do. A caseworker looking at a `0` must be able to find out it was inferred from a single character rather than read from the form.
- **Consider routing instead of silence.** Worth raising with the team: a coerced cell is a strong HITL candidate. The criteria node (§8.6) can flag "value was inferred, not read" as a review reason — you get the accuracy of the coercion *and* a human check, at a known workload cost. This does not change the benchmark numbers, only the review queue.

### 8.4 Evaluator changes

Two additions to `FieldMatchingRule` in [`schema-aware-evaluator.ts`](../../apps/temporal/src/evaluators/schema-aware-evaluator.ts):

**1. `maxEdits` on the fuzzy rule.** Today `fuzzy` is Levenshtein *ratio* only: `1 - distance/maxLen`. That is length-sensitive, and it's the wrong shape for OCR errors on short strings. `Lee` vs `Lei` is one substitution and scores 0.67 — below any sane threshold — while the same single substitution in a 30-character string scores 0.97. The offline normaliser therefore uses **two paths, either of which can match**:

- ratio ≥ 80 (catches paragraph-level drift on long strings), **OR**
- absolute edit distance ≤ N (catches single-character OCR errors uniformly, regardless of length)

with `N = 2` for names and `N = 4` for freeform, and a minimum-length floor of 3 on both paths so two-character strings can't degenerately match.

Port that faithfully:

```ts
{ rule: "fuzzy", fuzzyThreshold: 0.8, maxEdits: 2, minLength: 3 }
```

Match if `similarity >= fuzzyThreshold || (distance <= maxEdits && shorterLength >= minLength)`.

Note the deliberate looseness the report already documents for freeform: with `minLength 3` and `maxEdits 4`, unrelated 3–4 character strings can match. That is accepted because `explain_changes` gets LLM cleanup downstream. Keep the caveat in the doc comment.

**2. `canonicalize` on `FieldMatchingRule`** — per §5.2, a `FormatSpec` applied to both sides before comparison, reusing `field-format-engine`.

The resulting `evaluatorConfig`, which belongs in the SDPR workflow template's `metadata.evaluatorConfig`:

```jsonc
{
  "defaultRule": { "rule": "exact" },
  "passThreshold": 0.8,
  "fieldRules": {
    "signature":        { "rule": "presence" },
    "spouse_signature": { "rule": "presence" },
    "name":             { "rule": "fuzzy", "fuzzyThreshold": 0.8, "maxEdits": 2, "minLength": 3,
                          "canonicalize": { "canonicalize": "text|lowercase" } },
    "spouse_name":      { "rule": "fuzzy", "fuzzyThreshold": 0.8, "maxEdits": 2, "minLength": 3,
                          "canonicalize": { "canonicalize": "text|lowercase" } },
    "explain_changes":  { "rule": "fuzzy", "fuzzyThreshold": 0.8, "maxEdits": 4, "minLength": 3,
                          "canonicalize": { "canonicalize": "text|lowercase" } },
    "sin":              { "rule": "exact",   "canonicalize": { "canonicalize": "digits" } },
    "spouse_sin":       { "rule": "exact",   "canonicalize": { "canonicalize": "digits" } },
    "phone":            { "rule": "exact",   "canonicalize": { "canonicalize": "digits" } },
    "spouse_phone":     { "rule": "exact",   "canonicalize": { "canonicalize": "digits" } },
    "case_id":          { "rule": "exact",   "canonicalize": { "canonicalize": "strip-spaces|uppercase" } },
    "date":             { "rule": "date" },
    "spouse_date":      { "rule": "date" }
    // income fields: { "rule": "numeric" } — set via a pattern/default if per-field entries are unwieldy
    // checkbox_*: NO rule. Fixed at the representation layer (§5.1).
  }
}
```

Do **not** re-implement the standard precision/F1 formula — `develop` already has it (§4.3).

### 8.5 Ground-truth hygiene

Two known GT problems, both from report §10.6.3 and §5.1:

- **~10 cells where the engine is right and GT is wrong** (SIN, date, name, several checkboxes concentrated in one sample, spouse signature, one income cell). They inflate the error count by ~4%.
- **Checkbox tag representation** across all checkbox GT.

**Do not fix the first set during validation.** See §10.3 — the alignment target was computed against the current GT, warts included. Record them, fix them after alignment is signed off, and re-baseline explicitly.

The checkbox representation is different: it's a mechanical serialisation fix that the alignment *depends* on, and it changes no semantics. Do it in P5, and note it in the validation write-up as a deliberate, non-semantic GT change.

### 8.6 The HITL criteria node (the new feature)

**Activity:** `hitl.applyReviewCriteria` (name negotiable).
**Category:** OCR Quality / Validation.
**Position:** after all corrections, before the review switch.

**Purpose:** decide, per field, whether a human should look at it — and say why. Replaces the document-level average-confidence heuristic as the routing signal.

**Inputs:** the corrected OCR result ref; optionally `documentType` (template model id) so it can read the field schema for types and `format_spec` patterns.

**Parameters** (all generic; SDPR-ness lives in the values):

```jsonc
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "income-confidence-gate",
      "select": {
        "fieldPatterns": ["applicant_*", "spouse_*"],   // glob on field key
        "excludeFieldPatterns": ["*_name", "*_sin", "*_phone", "*_date", "*_signature"],
        "fieldTypes": ["number"]                        // or explicit "fields": [...]
      },
      "when": [
        { "confidenceBelow": 0.96 }
      ],
      "skipWhen": [
        { "predictionIsBlank": true },
        { "predictionLengthAtMost": 1 }
      ],
      "action": "review",
      "reason": "low-confidence income value"
    },
    {
      "name": "sin-confidence-gate",
      "select": { "fields": ["sin", "spouse_sin"] },
      "when": [{ "confidenceBelow": 0.90 }],
      "skipWhen": [{ "predictionIsBlank": true }],
      "action": "review",
      "reason": "low-confidence identifier"
    },
    {
      "name": "format-validation-failure",
      "select": { "fields": ["sin", "spouse_sin", "phone", "spouse_phone"] },
      "when": [{ "formatValidationFails": true }],
      "action": "review",
      "reason": "value does not match the expected format"
    }
  ],
  "defaultAction": "skip"
}
```

**Condition vocabulary** (start here; extend only when a real need appears):

| Condition | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `confidenceBelow: n` | field confidence < n |
| `predictionIsBlank: true` | prediction empty/null |
| `predictionLengthAtMost: n` | trimmed prediction length ≤ n |
| `formatValidationFails: true` | canonicalised value fails the field's `format_spec` pattern |
| `valueOutsideRange: {min,max}` | numeric sanity bounds (report §5.5, §7.3) |
| `valueWasInferred: true` | a correction step wrote this value rather than the OCR reading it (§8.3, and zero recovery) |
| `always: true` | unconditional review (report §5.5 recommends this shape for non-zero declared income) |

**Rules are prediction-side only.** No condition may consult ground truth. This is what makes the same configuration valid in benchmark and in production, and it is a hard constraint — see §10.2 for the consequence.

**Outputs:**

- `reviewPlan`: `[{ field, decision: "review"|"skip", reason, ruleName, confidence }]` — one entry per evaluated field
- `requiresReview`: boolean (any field marked `review`)
- `reviewFieldCount`, and counts grouped by rule name — these are what you compare against `hitl-per-category.csv`

**Configurability of the operating point (answering "should be able to choose").** Expose the thresholds as `exposedParams` on the node group. That makes them settable per benchmark definition via `workflowConfigOverrides` *without editing the workflow*, which in turn means the entire §3.4 recall ladder becomes **six benchmark definitions over one workflow version** — the in-app equivalent of the planner's sweep, and a genuinely nice validation artifact.

**Benchmark mode.** Benchmark documents must never park on a human gate — `ocr.checkConfidence` already special-cases document ids starting with `benchmark-`. The criteria node must **still run and still emit its plan and counts** in benchmark mode (that's how you validate the HITL numbers); only the *gate* is bypassed. Make sure the switch, not the criteria node, is where the benchmark short-circuit lives.

**Deliverables:** activity + unit tests, both activity registries, parameter schema registry, graph schema validator entry, node catalog documentation, and a `docs-md/` page under the HITL or workflows topic.

### 8.7 Making the review screen honour the plan

Today `HitlService.getSession()` returns every `keyValuePairs` entry and the workspace renders all of them, sorted by confidence.

Changes needed:

1. **Persist the plan.** The workflow computes it; the review session needs it. Store `reviewPlan` on the document (a JSON column, with a migration) so both the queue and the session can read it. Follow the repo's transaction and audit rules: the write is part of the workflow's document-update transaction, and it is a user-visible mutation, so it records an audit event.
2. **Return it from `getSession`** alongside the existing `fieldDefinitions`.
3. **Render it.** Default the workspace to *flagged fields only*, each showing its reason ("low-confidence income value", "failed format validation", "value inferred from a checkbox mark"). Keep a toggle to reveal all fields — reviewers must always be able to see the whole document, they just shouldn't have to.
4. **Backward path.** Documents with no plan (older, or workflows without the node) fall back to today's show-everything behaviour. That's not a compatibility shim to maintain forever — it's the honest meaning of "no policy configured".

Note that PR #184 (E09, draft) reworks this same review workspace — inline editing, snippet view, canvas overlay, confidence indicators. **Coordinate before touching `ReviewWorkspacePage.tsx`**, or you'll spend the time twice.

### 8.8 Simulated ICM handoff

**Decision: the workflow terminates in a simulated ICM handoff**, after the human gate — or directly, when criteria configuration says the document needs no review.

ICM is the ministry's case-management system; real integration is Deloitte's scope and explicitly out of scope for the report (§2.2). "Simulated" means: **produce and persist exactly the payload that would be sent, and don't send it.**

Build it from existing generic parts — there is no HTTP/webhook activity on `develop`, and this ticket is not the place to add one:

- **`data.transform`** renders the final field set into the ICM-shaped payload (JSON or XML) via field-mapping bindings.
- Persist the payload as a document artifact and set a terminal status via `document.updateStatus`.
- Optionally, **`tables.lookup`** against a seeded reference table stands in for the ICM *lookup* side — SIN → canonical case record — which lets you exercise the cross-validation concept the report leans on (§7.1) without any external dependency.

**Design for the routing the report anticipates.** Both branches must converge on the handoff, and the shape must not block what's coming:

- routing on **signature presence** (is the form signed at all?)
- routing on a **name match against an external system** (does the OCR'd name resemble the canonical name ICM returns for that SIN?)

These are workflow-level concepts, not evaluator concepts. Nothing in this ticket needs to implement them — but make sure the criteria node's structured, reason-carrying output and the switch's condition vocabulary can express `signature_present == false` or `icmNameMatch == false` as a branch when the time comes. If a design choice here would make that awkward, choose differently.

## 9. Data, environments, and handling sensitive material

### 9.1 What you need from the network share

Everything lives under:

```
\\widget\SDPRDocuments\convert_sd0081\100-doc\2026-05-05 performance report\
```

| File / folder | What it is | Why you need it | PII? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `benchmark-result.json` | V1 template export | baseline column in comparisons | **yes** (GT + predictions) |
| `benchmark-result-neural.json` | **V2 strict** — raw backend export | the "before" your workflow must improve on | **yes** |
| `benchmark-result-neural-normalized.json` | **V2 current** — the report's headline | **the target you must reproduce** | **yes** |
| `benchmark-result-neural-normalized.changes.csv` | one row per flipped cell, with rule name | **the per-cell spec of everything you're porting** — your P0 sizing and your reconciliation ledger | **yes** (carries values) |
| `benchmark-result-neural-normalized.md` | `analyze.js` summary | equals report appendix §11.3 | **yes** |
| `ocr-cache-dfaddb26/` | raw Azure poll response, one file per sample | **required** for zero-recovery work and for deterministic replay | **yes** |
| `plots/*.csv` | `aggregate-metrics`, `error-class-breakdown`, `per-category-accuracy`, `per-field-results`, `threshold-sweep`, `recommended-thresholds` | the §10.2–10.4 numbers, machine-readable | aggregates — low risk |
| `hitl/hitl-per-category.csv`, `hitl/hitl-combined.csv` | the §10.5 ladder | HITL validation target | aggregates — low risk |
| `hitl/hitl-curves.png` | the trade-off chart | context | no |
| `reports/wrong-by-category.csv` | every non-matched cell with predicted/expected/confidence, plus baseline context | investigating individual failures | **yes** |
| `reports/missing-comparison.csv` | per-cell missing-error comparison vs baseline | investigating the missing-class delta | **yes** |
| `reports/wrong-by-category-annotated.csv` | the above + manual failure-mode notes | §10.6 categorisation | **yes** |
| `reports/wrong-by-category-annotated-no-pii.csv` | PII-stripped variant | **prefer this one** for §10.6 work | no |

The benchmark run id for the neural run is `dfaddb26-cf91-4afa-aef8-c1ddeec42cc1` (the cache folder is named after its short prefix).

**Handling rule:** the PII-bearing files are production case data. They stay on the share. Don't copy them to your laptop, don't paste their contents into a terminal, a chat, a ticket or an AI tool. Aggregate counts and rule names are fine to share; values, sample IDs and per-cell rows are not.

### 9.2 Working locally without sensitive data on disk

Final validation runs against production (§9.3), but you need a fast local loop. Three complementary mechanisms already exist:

**(a) RAM-only streaming for share data.** The existing wrappers in `scripts/benchmark analysis/*-share.sh` already implement this pattern and are the model to copy:

- **Input:** PowerShell `ReadAllBytes` writes into a **named pipe (FIFO)**; Python reads the FIFO like a file. The FIFO is a zero-byte filesystem node — the bytes travel through kernel pipe buffers in RAM and never land on disk.
- **Output:** written to **`/dev/shm`** (tmpfs — RAM-backed), then PowerShell-copied to the share, then the tmpfs subtree is deleted on exit.
- Output FIFOs deadlock (both sides block on open), which is why outputs go through `/dev/shm` rather than a second pipe. Don't "simplify" that away.

The same shape works for anything else you need to pull off the share.

**(b) Local-folder dataset seeding.** `data/datasets/<name>/{public,private}/` is scanned on dev backend start, seeded as a `Dataset` + `DatasetVersion`, and synced to blob storage ([local-datasets-seeding.md](../local-datasets-seeding.md)). Supports either a curated `manifest.json` or flat `<name>.jpg` + `<name>.json` pairs.

To combine (a) and (b) without persisting production data: point `data/datasets/<name>` at a **tmpfs directory** (a symlink into `/dev/shm`, or a `tmpfs` mount) that you populate per session from the share. You get the full local benchmark loop; a reboot — or a `rm -rf` on exit — wipes it, and nothing was ever written to persistent disk. Make sure `data/datasets/**` is gitignored for real (verify before the first copy, not after).

**(c) Synthetic/de-identified data for day-to-day work.** Most of what you're building — the criteria node's rule engine, the fuzzy-match changes, the format specs, the handoff step — can be developed and unit-tested against fixtures with no real content at all. Reserve real data for the alignment runs. Prefer this by default: it's faster, and it's the only approach with no handling risk.

**Server-side OCR cache export.** `scripts/oc-export-benchmark-ocr-cache.sh` streams cache rows from the production DB pod straight to a UNC destination, base64 over a pipe, one file per sample. No payload bytes touch the WSL filesystem, and neither payloads nor sample IDs are logged. Use it as-is if you need to refresh the cache; use it as the template if you need a similar export.

### 9.3 The validation run

Runs on **production** at the end, because that's where the 99-document dataset with its ground truth lives.

Use **OCR cache replay**: `CreateRunDto` accepts `ocrCacheBaselineRunId`. Point it at `dfaddb26-…` and the run replays the cached Azure responses instead of calling Azure again.

Why this matters: Azure is not deterministic. A fresh call against the neural model can return slightly different values and confidences, which would blur the thing you're trying to measure. Replay holds the OCR input byte-identical to what produced the report, so **any difference in the output is your post-processing, and nothing else**. That is the only clean way to prove the port is faithful.

Then do a second, **live** run without the cache. Its numbers will differ slightly, and that's expected and fine — it demonstrates the workflow works operationally end to end, which is the other half of the ticket.

## 10. Validation protocol

### 10.1 The procedure

1. Create a benchmark definition: the 99-doc dataset version, your new workflow version pinned, `evaluatorType: schema-aware`, the `evaluatorConfig` from §8.4.
2. Run it with `ocrCacheBaselineRunId = dfaddb26-…`.
3. Download the export: `GET /api/benchmark/projects/:projectId/runs/:runId/download`.
4. Feed it **straight** into the existing analysis tooling — with **no `normalize-benchmark.py` and no `recover-numeric-zeros.py` step**:

   ```bash
   python3 "scripts/benchmark analysis/compare-engines.py" \
       "Neural V2 current (report)=<share>/benchmark-result-neural-normalized.json" \
       "Workflow (in-app)=<your-export>.json" \
       --out-dir <out> --docs-count 99
   ```

   The whole point: those two columns should now be the same. If reproducing the report's post-processing inside the workflow worked, the raw export already *is* the normalised result.
5. For HITL, run `hitl-planner.py` on your export with the report's flags, and separately compare against your criteria node's own emitted counts:

   ```bash
   python3 "scripts/benchmark analysis/hitl-planner.py" <your-export>.json \
       --out-dir <out> --categories income_amounts,sin \
       --exclude-missing-in-categories income_amounts \
       --skip-trivial-predictions-in-categories income_amounts
   ```

6. **Reconcile per cell, not just per aggregate.** Matching totals can hide two errors cancelling out. Use `report-errors.py` to produce `wrong-by-category.csv` for your run, diff it against the report's, and account for every differing row. The audit CSV from P0 is your ledger.

### 10.2 Expected divergence 1 — the sin workload column

**Short version:** the report's `sin reviews / 100 docs` numbers were computed with a filter that peeks at the ground truth. Your production code can't do that, so your sin workload will differ. This is a defect in the measurement, not in your implementation — but you must call it out rather than let it read as a mismatch.

**The detail.** "Reviews per 100 docs" is meant to count only predictions where a human has actual work to do. If a cell is blank on the form *and* the model returned blank, there's nothing to verify — counting it would inflate the workload with non-work. `hitl-planner.py` implements this with two different filters:

- **For income** (`--skip-trivial-predictions-in-categories income_amounts`) it uses `_reviewable_skip_trivial`, which looks **only at the prediction**: blank, or a single character ⇒ skip. Nothing about the correct answer is consulted. **This one is production-implementable.**
- **For sin** (no such flag) it falls back to `_reviewable_default`, which excludes a cell when **both the prediction and the ground truth are empty**. That second half is the problem: at decision time in production you do not know whether the cell is blank on the form. You only know the model returned nothing.

So the report's sin workload excludes "both blank" cells but *keeps* "model blank, form had a value" cells — the missing-class errors. A production rule can only see "the prediction is blank" and would drop both groups. The two counts therefore differ by exactly the number of flagged sin **missing** errors.

Concretely, on a form with a single applicant, `spouse_sin` is legitimately blank: no prediction, no GT, no work. The report correctly excludes it. Your node also excludes it — but by the rule "the prediction is blank", which *also* excludes the case where the applicant did write a SIN and the model missed it. The report counts that one as review work; you can't distinguish it.

**What to do:**

1. Implement the prediction-only rule. The alternative is a rule that can't run in production, which defeats the ticket.
2. Quantify the gap: count flagged sin cells with a blank prediction at each threshold. Report it as an explicit line item.
3. Note the direction: your workload numbers will be **slightly lower** than §10.5.1's for sin, because you drop cells the report counts. Income is unaffected — its filter was already prediction-only.
4. Feed it back: the report's sin column is arguably measuring something not achievable operationally, and a future revision should use the prediction-only filter for every category so the published number is the one an operations team would actually see.

### 10.3 Expected divergence 2 — the ground truth must be frozen

**Short version:** the report's targets are computed against a specific, imperfect snapshot of the ground truth. If anyone edits that ground truth while you're validating, every target number moves and you'll be chasing a moving reference.

**The detail.** Every number in §3 is `matched cells ÷ evaluated cells` against the GT as it stood when the report was generated. That GT contains known errors — report §10.6.3 found **about 10 cells where the engine returned the correct value and the GT itself is wrong**, spread across SIN, date, name, several checkboxes concentrated in one sample, spouse signature, and one income cell. They inflate the reported error count by roughly 4% (10 of 267).

The report is upfront that these should be cleaned up before V3, and estimates true accuracy is nearer 96.5% than 96.4%. That cleanup is correct — and it is **poison during validation**. Suppose you fix five of them mid-flight: your run now shows 262 errors against a 267 target. Is that your workflow doing something wrong, or the GT fix? Without a per-cell ledger you cannot tell, and you will burn days on it.

The same applies to anything else that shifts the reference: re-labelling, adding or dropping samples, or creating a new dataset version.

**What to do:**

1. **Pin the dataset version** used for the report and run every alignment benchmark against that exact version. Dataset versions are immutable snapshots — use that property.
2. **Freeze it socially too.** Tell whoever owns labelling that this version is a validation reference and must not be edited. Someone "helpfully" fixing ten obviously-wrong cells is the realistic failure mode.
3. **Fix the GT after sign-off, not before.** Then create a *new* dataset version, re-run, and record both numbers — "96.4% on frozen v1, 96.5% on corrected v2" — so the improvement is attributed to the GT fix rather than confused with a workflow change.
4. **One exception, deliberately taken:** the checkbox representation fix (§5.1). It changes serialisation, not meaning, and the alignment can't work without it. Document it as such in the write-up.

### 10.4 Deltas you should expect, and the tolerance

| Source | Expected effect | Acceptable? |
|---|---|---|
| `date-month-day-swap` dropped (§5.3) | small drop in `date` category | yes — quantify it |
| sin workload filter (§10.2) | sin reviews/100 slightly lower | yes — quantify it |
| checkbox representation fix (§5.1) | none, if done right | must net to zero |
| Live (non-replay) run | small drift across the board | yes — expected, report separately |
| Anything else | — | **no.** Reconcile per cell. |

With cache replay and a frozen dataset the pipeline is deterministic, so aim for **exact** agreement on the error counts in §3.2, minus the two documented deltas. "Close enough" is not the bar — every differing cell should have a name.

## 11. Decisions already made

Recorded so you don't re-litigate them. All confirmed by Alex on 2026-07-29.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Base branch | **`develop`.** No visual builder, no dynamic nodes. Author workflows as JSON. |
| 2 | Workflow/evaluator split (§5) | Approved. **Note:** future routing on signature presence and on name-match against an external system are *workflow* concepts — design so they fit (§8.8). |
| 3 | Single-char income → `0` in production | **Option (a): do it in the workflow.** Matches the report exactly. Audit every coercion (§8.3). |
| 4 | Canonicalisation vs GT | **Option (a): symmetric `canonicalize` in the evaluator.** Rationale in §5.2. Exception: checkboxes fixed at source. |
| 5 | `date-month-day-swap` | **Drop it.** Measure and report the cost (§5.3). |
| 6 | HITL criteria scope | Per-field rules with pattern/type selectors; both "which fields are shown" and "does this document need review" (§8.6). |
| 7 | Operating point (target recall) | **Selectable**, not hard-coded. Exposed params → overridable per benchmark definition (§8.6). |
| 8 | Where criteria are configured | **On the workflow node.** Travels with the workflow, benchmarkable, versioned. |
| 9 | Environment | Final validation on **production**. Local dev via tmpfs/RAM-only handling + local dataset seeding (§9.2). |
| 10 | Where the workflow ends | **Simulated ICM handoff** after HITL — or directly, when criteria say no review is needed (§8.8). |
